segments.heading: Header comment: what the script does
segments.text: The comment states what the script does. It repeats the 120-thread part of `run_kernels.sh` with the two binaries of 2026-11-13 and builds nothing. `bw_old` holds the old read kernel. `bw_new` holds the new read kernel.

- `-e`: the script stops at the first command that fails (exit status not 0). A failing command inside an `if` test or in front of `||` does not stop it.
- `-u`: the script stops when it uses a variable that was never set.
- `-o pipefail`: a pipeline (commands joined with `|`) counts as failed when any command of it fails, not only the last one.

segments.heading: Restart on CPUs 0 to 119
segments.text:
- The script starts itself again under `taskset -c 0-119`. This tool limits a command to CPUs 0 to 119.
- `exec` replaces the running shell with that command. No extra process is created.
- `_PINNED=1` is set for the new start. The test `-z ${_PINNED:-}` (is the variable empty or not set?) is then false. So the restart happens only once.
- Every process that the script starts later inherits the CPU limit. The benchmark binaries are among them.

`NAME` is the first argument. If it is missing or empty, bash prints `usage: ra.sh NAME` and the script ends with status 1. `NAME` becomes part of the name of the result folder (line 22). go.sh passes `T72A1`, `T72A2` and `T72A3`, one per session [Ref4].

segments.heading: Function `check_marker`: stop when another test runs
segments.text: `check_marker` tests whether the marker file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` exists (`-e`). If it exists, the function prints a message to the error output (stderr, `>&2`) and ends the script with status 3. Line 13 is the first call.

segments.heading: Check that the binaries are those of 2026-11-13
segments.text:
- `SRC` is the folder on CRB that holds `bw_old` and `bw_new`.
- `sha256sum -c -` reads the two lines between `<<'SUMS'` and `SUMS`. Each line holds a checksum and a file name. The tool computes the sha256 of each file and compares it with the given value.
- `> /dev/null` drops the report of the tool. Only its exit status is used.
- The parentheses run `cd` and the check in a subshell (a child copy of the shell). The working folder of the script itself does not change.
- If a file differs or cannot be read, the part after `||` runs: the script prints `sha mismatch ...` and ends with status 2.
- The two checksums equal the values that `run_kernels.sh` recorded for the binaries on 2026-11-13 [Ref1].

- `TS` is the UTC time of this moment, written as date, `T`, time, `Z`. In session 1 it was `20261117T221209Z` [Ref3].
- `OUT` is the result folder: `k120-`, then `NAME`, then `TS`, under `$HOME/cache-perf/results`. `mkdir -p` creates it.
- The time is read before the wait of lines 26 to 28. So the first process starts at least 5 s after the time in the folder name.

segments.heading: Function `load`: the three load averages
segments.text: Function `load` prints the first three fields of `/proc/loadavg` (`cut -d' ' -f1-3`: split the line at spaces and keep fields 1 to 3). They are the load averages over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

segments.heading: Wait until at most 2 tasks are runnable
segments.text:
- Line 26: the loop runs at most 40 times. Each time it reads the fourth field of `/proc/loadavg`, which holds two numbers with a slash between them. The second `cut` keeps the number before the slash. This is `r`, the number of tasks that are runnable now.
- If `r` is 2 or less, `break` leaves the loop. If not, the script sleeps 1 s and reads again.
- Line 27: if `r` is still above 2 after the 40 readings, the script ends with status 6.
- Line 28: the script then always waits 5 s more.
- Line 29: the marker file is checked again after the wait.
- This wait runs once, before the first of the 24 processes. rx.sh has the same loop and the same 5 s wait before every process, but not the stop of line 27 [Ref5].

segments.heading: Write the machine state to `probe.txt`
segments.text:
- The braces group lines 31 to 35. `> "$OUT/probe.txt"` writes the output of all of them to the new file `probe.txt`.
- Line 31: host name, UTC time, load averages, number of login sessions (`who` prints one line per login session, `wc -l` counts the lines) and `NAME`.
- Line 32: the boot id, the `MemTotal` line of `/proc/meminfo` (`tr -s ' '` turns each run of spaces into one space) and the last value of `r`. The script read this value in the loop of line 26, before the 5 s wait.
- Line 33: the release of the Linux kernel (`uname -r`) and the setting for transparent huge pages. The value in square brackets is the active one.
- Line 34: `ps -eo pcpu,user,comm --sort=-pcpu` lists all processes with their %CPU, user and command name, highest %CPU first. `head -6` keeps the title line and 5 processes.
- Line 35: the sha256 of `bw_old`, of `bw_new` and of this script (`$0`).

segments.heading: Function `one`: start one benchmark process
segments.text:
- Arguments in this order: csv file, binary, kernel, threads, CPU list, bytes, round.
- Line 40: check the marker file before every process. Nothing checks it while a process runs.
- Line 41: append one line that starts with `-- ` to the csv file. It holds the arguments, the 1-minute load average at this moment and the UTC time. stat_k120.py reads this line to know which rows belong to which process [Ref6].
- Line 42: start the binary with one kernel (`--kernel`) and wait until it ends. `>>` appends the rows that the binary prints to the csv file.
- `--reps 3`: the process times 3 intervals. `--min-ms 500`: each interval lasts at least 500 ms [Ref2].
- If the binary ends with a status other than 0, `set -e` ends the script with that status.

`K1` is the kernel order of round 1. `K2` holds the same six names in the reverse order, for round 2. `read` and `asmread` are the read kernels, and the other four names are the write and copy kernels. A `for` loop over such a list takes the names one by one.

segments.heading: The 24 processes: round 1, then round 2 in reverse order
segments.text:
- Round 1 (`BINS` holds old, then new, and `KS` is `K1`): for each kernel first `bw_old`, then `bw_new`. Order: old `read`, new `read`, old `write`, new `write`, old `copy`, new `copy`, old `asmread`, new `asmread`, old `asmwrite`, new `asmwrite`, old `asmcopy`, new `asmcopy`.
- Round 2 (`BINS` holds new, then old, and `KS` is `K2`): the exact reverse of round 1. Order: new `asmcopy`, old `asmcopy`, new `asmwrite`, old `asmwrite`, new `asmread`, old `asmread`, new `copy`, old `copy`, new `write`, old `write`, new `read`, old `read`.
- Every process gets the same arguments: 120 threads and the CPU list `0-119`. The binary pins thread number i to CPU i. `256M` gives each thread its own buffer of 256 MiB. Each process times 3 intervals of at least 500 ms each [Ref2].
- All 24 processes append to one file, `threads120.csv`.
- No wait separates two processes. Only the first process (old `read`, round 1) starts directly after the wait of lines 26 to 28.
- The new read kernel starts directly after the old read kernel in round 1. In round 2 it starts directly after `bw_old` with `write`, and the old read kernel is the last process.
Line 49 appends a last line to `probe.txt`: the load averages, the UTC time and the `MemTotal` line after the last process. Line 50 prints `done` and the result folder.
